newsitem.title: USA: Babbitt signs changes in Grand Canyon flows.
newsitem.headline: Babbitt signs changes in Grand Canyon flows.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt Wednesday launched what he called a new era at the Grand Canyon, signing a measure that restricts the waters that flow through the famed gorge.
At a ceremony in Phoenix, Babbitt formally signed a document that will make permanent changes in the operation of Glen Canyon Dam to protect the downstream environment.

The changes, which have been more than a decade in the making, mean that the flows from the dam into the Colorado River no longer will be regulated only by the need for water and cheap hydroelectric power.
Instead, Babbitt said protecting the natural vegetation, wildlife and Native American artifacts in the vast canyon will carry a hefty weight.
"This hereby mandates that we will flood this river into perpetuity for the benefit of all parties," he said.
Babbitt said the results of a man-made flood of the canyon in March proved that the canyon's natural surroundings could be brought back with proper management of the dam.

"The hypothesis is now fact," he told reporters at a local desert botanical garden. "That is, the Grand Canyon has been greatly restored and enhanced into something resembling its original condition."
The former Arizona governor said the new management plan strikes a good balance between different canyon users.
A report released Wednesday showed that the week-long flood in March had dramatic effects along the 277-mile-long canyon.
More and higher beaches were created, rapids were brought back to life and endangered fish habitats swelled by 20 percent. Additionally, nutrient-rich sediment was returned.
These elements had been eroding since Glen Canyon was built in 1963, in an attempt to harness the river to meet the needs of millions of people across the growing Southwest.

Early on, the need for power meant high flows early in the day and trickles during the evening. It also meant 90 percent of the rich sediment that it once carried remained trapped behind the dam's wall.
What was once a warm silt-laden flow was transformed into a cold and clear green stream.

The moves set off an environmental chain-reaction that saw the beaches erode, and natural vegetation and wildlife begin to disappear. In its place came fish and trees that were previously strangers to the area.
The erosion also meant the river-rafting - a popular canyon activity -- was disrupted and rafters were forced to look harder for places in which to camp.

In the last several years, reductions in the amount and timing of the water releases have been made to help satisfy environmental concerns. They have drawn opposition by power administrators, who say the restrictions are costing them tens of millions of dollars.
